newsitem.title: USA: Eye drug helps AIDS-related vision problems.
newsitem.headline: Eye drug helps AIDS-related vision problems.

text.p: People suffering from AIDS risk developing an eye infection that can progress to blindness, but doctors have found a better way to treat the infection by implating a time-release drug tablet into the eye itself.

In a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, researcher David Musch of the University of Michigan and his colleagues say the way to treat the cytomegalovirus retinitis infection is with the well-established drug ganciclovir.

In a test designed to find the best way to give the medicine, 56 volunteers got it intravenously, 62 received implants that slowly released the drug into the infected eye and 55 got implants that released it twice as fast.
The implants, actually coated disk-shaped pellets, were surgically anchored to the white of the eye in a way that let the implant float in the gelatin-like fluid behind the lens.

Those that released the drug at a rate of one microgram per hour prevented the retinitis from progressing for an average of 221 days. Implants with the higher dose kept the condition at bay for nearly as long. In contrast, volunteers who got the intravenous form of the drug saw their eye problems get worse after an average of only 71 days.
"The risk of progression of retinitis was almost three times as great among patients treated with intravenous ganciclovir as among those treated with a ganciclovir implant," the researchers said.
The results "demonstrate a substantial and clinically important benefit" to using the implant, they concluded.

However, there was a drawback to treatment with the implants. The team discovered that people with the implants were more likely to have the retinitis spread to the unaffected eye. Apparently the intravenous treatments with ganciclovir were more effective at keeping the virus away from the healthy eye.
One solution to that problem, Musch told Reuters, may be to give patients oral ganciclovir at the same time the implant is in place.

The other side effect of the treatment was cloudy vision in the eye with the implant. The reason, Musch explained, is that blood from the surgery can get into the fluid behind the lens. But the problem cleared up in a few weeks as the eye absorbed the blood and vision returned to normal.

The implants are sold under the brand name Vitrasert by Chiron Vision Corp., a unit of Chiron Corp. Ganciclovir is sold under the brand name Cytovene by Hoffmann-La Roche Laboratories in Nutley, N.J., a subsidiary of Roche Holdings, Ltd.
